title: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
metaTitle: What Are Mineral Rights Worth in Pennsylvania?
metaDescription: What actually drives mineral rights value in Pennsylvania, from formation and county activity to lease terms and deductions, without a fake price promise.
heroLead: Every family wants a number, and every honest answer starts with it depends, which frustrates everyone including us.
intro: We know how unsatisfying it is to ask what your minerals are worth and hear a list of factors instead of a figure. But anyone giving you a firm number before looking at your deed and, if there's production, your royalty statements is skipping steps that actually determine the answer. What we can do here is walk through what genuinely drives value in Pennsylvania, so when a real number does come your way, you understand why it's what it is.
Our own family sat through this same conversation before we sold part of our interest, and the factors below are the ones that actually moved the number, not the ones people assume matter most.

sections.heading: Formation, depth, and where you sit in the play
paragraphs: Pennsylvania sits over the Marcellus shale broadly and the deeper Utica in parts of the southwest, and where your acreage falls within those formations matters enormously. Core areas of the northeast Marcellus, counties like Susquehanna, Bradford, and Sullivan, have historically seen some of the strongest well results in the state. Southwest counties like Washington and Greene see activity in both the Marcellus and the deeper, more expensive Utica. Acreage on the flank of the play, or in counties with thinner pay zones, typically sees less operator interest, which affects both lease bonus potential and sale value.

This isn't a judgment on any particular piece of ground, it's simply how operators allocate capital, and it varies with rig count and commodity prices year to year, so activity picture in your county today isn't necessarily where it'll be in five years.

sections.heading: Lease status and production history
paragraphs: Unleased acreage with no nearby drilling carries more speculative value than a producing well with two years of clean royalty statements behind it. If you're leased but undrilled, the terms of that lease, royalty fraction, primary term remaining, whether it has a no-deductions clause, all factor into what a buyer will pay, because they're effectively stepping into your shoes under that agreement.

If there's an active well, decline curve and recent monthly volumes matter more than almost anything else, since they let a buyer project future income with some confidence instead of guessing from county averages.

sections.heading: Why we won't quote a flat number without your paperwork
paragraphs: Any value talk that isn't tied to your actual deed, acreage, and production varies with activity and commodity prices, and treating it otherwise sets up a number that won't survive a real review of your statements. We'd rather walk through your paperwork and give you a figure grounded in your own situation than throw out a range that sounds good on a landing page and falls apart at the table.

If you're comparing offers, ask each buyer the same question: what specifically in my paperwork led to this number. A real answer references your county's recent activity, your decline curve if you have one, and your lease terms if applicable.

sections.heading: A note on the checks we've watched shrink
paragraphs: Our family's own royalty checks looked strong the first couple years after the well came online, then the decline curve did what decline curves do, and post-production deductions took a bigger bite as volumes fell. Watching that happen firsthand is part of why we don't like flat promises about value, because the honest answer changes as the well itself changes.

If you're weighing an offer against years of future royalty checks, ask yourself where your well likely sits on its own decline curve, and how the deductions on your recent statements compare to gross value. That comparison, more than any single number, is what actually tells you whether an offer looks reasonable.

faqs.question: Can you just give me a rough per-acre number over the phone?
faqs.answer: We can talk through the factors that drive value in your county, but a specific number depends on reviewing your deed, acreage, and any production or lease paperwork you have. Value varies with activity and isn't something we'll guess at blind.

faqs.question: Are minerals in the core of the Marcellus always worth more?
faqs.answer: Typically core areas see more operator interest and stronger well results, which supports higher lease and sale activity, but individual tract factors, lease terms, and deduction levels still matter within any county.

faqs.question: Does unleased acreage have any value if nothing's drilling nearby?
faqs.answer: It can, particularly if the formation quality and county activity trend suggest future interest, but it's a more speculative valuation than a producing interest with statements to review.

faqs.question: How do post-production deductions affect what my minerals are worth?
faqs.answer: Heavier deductions reduce the net royalty income a buyer can expect from a producing interest, which lowers the value even when gross production is strong, so we always ask to see recent statements.

faqs.question: Do Act 13 impact fees affect what my minerals are worth?
faqs.answer: Not directly, since the impact fee is paid by the operator to the county, not deducted from your royalty. It's more useful as context for how active drilling is in your county than as a factor in your own valuation.
